title: UnitedHealthcare Humana Medicare Advantage Cancellations

sections.text: What's Happening With UnitedHealthcare and Humana Medicare Advantage Plans

sections.content: For 2026, UnitedHealthcare and Humana have pulled back from certain Medicare Advantage plans and service areas, a shift affecting roughly one million enrollees nationwide. If your plan is one of those being discontinued, you will receive a non-renewal or termination notice directly from your insurer.

Insurers typically exit a county or end a specific plan when rising medical costs, low enrollment, or thin provider networks make the plan difficult to sustain at a competitive price. These business decisions are made plan by plan, so a cancellation in one county does not necessarily mean the same insurer is leaving a neighboring one.

The surest way to find out whether your plan is affected is to check the notice letter mailed by your carrier, call the number on your member ID card, or use the [Medicare Plan Finder](https://www.medicare.gov/) to confirm your plan's status for next year.

sections.text: The One Essential Step You Need to Take Right Now

sections.content: If your Medicare Advantage plan is being discontinued, the single most important action is confirming two dates: the day your current plan actually ends and the start and end of your Special Enrollment Period. These dates determine how much time you have to pick new coverage without a gap.

Acting early matters because a lapse in coverage can interrupt access to your doctors and, more urgently, your prescriptions. Pharmacies will not process claims under a plan that has already ended, and switching plans takes time to process once you enroll.

items: Your plan termination notice, which states your exact end date
Your current Medicare plan ID and Medicare number
A list of your doctors and specialists, including their locations
A current list of your medications, dosages, and pharmacy

sections.calloutText: Keep your termination notice somewhere easy to find. It lists your plan's exact end date and often includes a summary of your enrollment rights, which you will need when comparing new plans.

sections.text: Understanding Your Special Enrollment Period Timeline

sections.content: When Medicare or an insurer ends your plan involuntarily, you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) that is separate from the Annual Enrollment Period that runs from October 15 to December 7. This SEP gives you a dedicated window to pick new coverage outside the standard calendar.

According to [Medicare's Special Enrollment Period rules](https://www.medicare.gov/), you generally have a window of time both before and after your plan's termination date to choose new coverage, though exact timing can depend on how the notice was issued. Missing this window can leave you temporarily defaulted into Original Medicare with no drug coverage, which may expose you to a Part D late enrollment penalty down the road.

If you do not actively choose a new plan, Medicare or your insurer may automatically reassign you to a similar plan to avoid a coverage gap. This default option is not always the best fit for your doctors or medications, so reviewing your choices yourself, rather than relying on automatic reassignment, gives you more control over the outcome.

sections.text: How to Compare New Medicare Advantage or Medicare Options Without Feeling Overwhelmed

sections.content: Rather than comparing every plan detail at once, break your review into three categories: your doctors, your prescriptions, and your total expected costs. This narrows a long list of plans down to the few that genuinely fit your situation.

A low monthly premium does not tell you the whole story. Two plans with similar premiums can have very different deductibles, copays, and out-of-pocket maximums, and the 2026 maximum out-of-pocket limit for Medicare Advantage plans is $9,250, though individual plans often set lower limits. Looking only at the premium can mean missing a plan with higher costs once you actually need care.

sections.text: Will Your Doctors and Specialists Still Be Covered?

sections.content: Before enrolling in any new plan, check its provider directory to confirm your current doctors and specialists are included. Directories can be outdated, so it also helps to call the doctor's office directly and ask whether they are accepting new patients under that specific plan.

If your preferred provider is not in any nearby plan's network, you may need to decide between switching doctors or switching to Original Medicare paired with a Medicare Supplement plan, which typically allows you to see any doctor who accepts Medicare.

Compare each new plan's drug formulary against your actual medication list, including dosages. A drug being covered is not the full picture; you also want to check which tier it falls under, since moving to a higher tier can raise your copay noticeably even if the drug itself remains covered.

For 2026, Part D plans carry a maximum deductible of $615, and once a member's out-of-pocket drug spending reaches the $2,100 catastrophic threshold, cost-sharing changes substantially. Reviewing these figures against a plan's specific drug list helps you estimate your real annual cost rather than relying on the premium alone.

Before you narrow your choices down to one plan, call each doctor's office and your pharmacy directly to confirm network and formulary status. Online directories are not always current, and a five-minute phone call can prevent a costly surprise after you have already enrolled.

sections.text: Avoiding Costly Mistakes During This Transition

sections.content: Under time pressure, it is common for people to pick a plan based on premium alone, skip checking the formulary tier of a key medication, or assume their doctor is in-network without confirming it. Any of these shortcuts can lead to higher bills or disrupted care once the new plan year begins.

Missing your SEP deadline can also create a gap in drug coverage, which may trigger a Part D late enrollment penalty based on the national base premium; for 2026, that penalty calculation uses a base beneficiary premium of $38.99. Marking your SEP end date somewhere visible, such as a calendar reminder, helps you avoid this outcome.

sections.calloutText: Letting your Special Enrollment Period lapse without choosing a plan can mean a gap in prescription coverage and possible late enrollment penalties. Confirm your exact deadline from your notice letter rather than assuming you have until the Annual Enrollment Period.

sections.content: Getting a second opinion before finalizing your choice, whether from a trusted family member, a State Health Insurance Assistance Program counselor, or a licensed agent, can catch a network or formulary issue you might have missed on your own.

A licensed Medicare agent can explain your available plan options, compare costs based on your doctors and medications, and walk you through enrollment paperwork. An agent cannot guarantee a specific plan will cover every cost, and they should always disclose which companies they represent.

Helpful guidance focuses on your specific situation and answers your questions directly, without pushing you toward a decision before you are ready. A sales pitch, by contrast, tends to emphasize urgency or a single plan without walking through alternatives.

items: They explain plan details in plain language, not just marketing terms
They disclose which insurance companies they are licensed to represent
They are willing to compare more than one plan option with you
They do not pressure you to enroll during the first conversation

faqs.question: I just received my cancellation notice. Do I need to decide today?
faqs.answer: No. Your Special Enrollment Period gives you a real window of time to review your options, typically spanning several weeks before and after your plan's end date. Rushing is not necessary if you start reviewing your notice and options soon after you receive it.

faqs.question: Will I get pushy sales calls if I ask about new plans?
faqs.answer: Licensed agents are expected to answer your questions and compare options without pressuring you into an immediate decision. You can set expectations upfront by telling an agent you want information only, or that you are comparing multiple sources before enrolling.

faqs.question: Can I just research this on my own instead of talking to someone?
faqs.answer: Yes, self-research works well for many people, especially using Medicare.gov's Plan Finder tool. Where self-research often falls short is confirming current network status or formulary tier details, since online directories can be outdated and a phone call to your doctor or pharmacy fills that gap.

faqs.question: How do I know which sources of Medicare information I can trust?
faqs.answer: Look for sources that explain plan details in plain language, disclose which insurers they represent, and do not pressure you toward one plan. Pairing official data from Medicare.gov with guidance from a licensed agent gives you both accuracy and a personalized comparison.

sections.text: Your Next Step Toward Confident Coverage

sections.content: The most urgent action this week is confirming your plan's termination date and your Special Enrollment Period deadline from your notice letter. From there, gather your doctor list, medication list, and plan information so you are ready to compare options.

Review your notice letter closely and start comparing new plans well before your deadline closes, rather than waiting until the final days of your enrollment window. If you would like a no-pressure comparison of plans available in your area, you can speak with a licensed Medicare agent who can walk through your doctors, prescriptions, and budget with you.
